items.stem: Explain the factors that increase the likelihood of slope failure.
items.answer: Steep slopes; weak, weathered or jointed rock; bedding dipping parallel to the slope; saturation and high pore pressure; removal of vegetation; undercutting by rivers, waves or road cuts; loading by buildings; earthquake shaking.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per factor [4]

items.stem: Explain how deforestation increases landslide risk.
items.answer: Roots that bind soil decay; interception and transpiration fall, so more water reaches and stays in the soil, raising pore pressure.

items.stem: Table 10.1 shows four rainstorms on a hillside in Nepal (duration in hours, mean intensity in mm/h): storm A: 12 h, 2.2 mm/h; storm B: 1 h, 11.9 mm/h; storm C: 1 h, 8.9 mm/h; storm D: 24 h, 9.4 mm/h. A global threshold for shallow landslides is I = 14.82 D^−0.39, where I is intensity (mm/h) and D is duration (h). Explain why the threshold intensity falls as storm duration increases.
items.answer: Long storms progressively saturate the soil and raise the water table, so a lower intensity is enough to raise pore-water pressure to the point of failure.

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that human activity is now the main cause of mass movement hazards.
items.answer: For: Deforestation, road building, quarrying, slope loading and informal settlements on steep slopes increase failures (Rio de Janeiro favelas, Hong Kong before 1977, Freetown 2017). Against: Natural factors (steep slopes, weak rocks, monsoon rain, earthquakes like Wenchuan 2008 or Nepal 2015) cause most landslides; humans mainly increase exposure. Conclusion: Natural factors are the underlying causes, but human activity increasingly triggers failures and, above all, puts people at risk.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “shear stress”?
options: The pressure of water in the spaces between soil particles, which reduces friction and strength.
Shear strength ÷ shear stress; a slope with a value below 1 is likely to fail.
The force acting to move material downslope, which increases with slope angle and weight.
The internal resistance of slope material to movement, from friction and cohesion.

items.stem: Explain why earthquakes trigger landslides.
items.answer: Shaking adds a horizontal force (increasing shear stress) and can cause liquefaction or fracturing that reduces shear strength.

items.stem: Explain the impacts of landslides on people in LICs.
items.answer: Deaths and injuries; destruction of homes in informal settlements on steep slopes; blocked roads and rivers (landslide dams); loss of farmland; disruption of water supplies; long recovery.

items.stem: “The impacts of mass movements depend more on human factors than on the type of movement.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to warning, vulnerability and speed.
items.answer: For: Vulnerability (poverty, informal housing on slopes, lack of warning, weak planning) explains high deaths in Freetown 2017 and Vargas 1999. Against: Fast movements such as debris flows, rock avalanches (Huascarán 1970) and mudflows kill far more than slow creep or slumps whatever the human situation. Conclusion: The type of movement sets the potential impact, but human vulnerability and exposure determine the actual losses.

items.stem: Explain how engineering can reduce landslide risk.
items.answer: Regrading to reduce slope angle; retaining walls and soil nails increase strength; drainage reduces pore pressure; rock bolts and netting stop rockfalls; vegetation binds soil.

items.stem: Fig. 10.3 shows the cumulative displacement (mm) recorded by an extensometer on a landslide above a village in the Swiss Alps: day 0: 0, day 7: 2.8, day 14: 4.9, day 21: 14.7, day 28: 21.7, day 35: 28.7. Engineers issue an alert when the rate of movement exceeds 1.5 mm per day. Suggest limitations of relying on one extensometer.
items.answer: It measures movement at only one point and at the surface; movement elsewhere or at depth may be missed; instrument failure; data need continuous checking.

items.stem: Outline the evidence that supports, and the evidence that challenges, the view that monitoring and warning are more effective than stabilisation in reducing mass movement risk.
items.answer: For: Monitoring (inclinometers, InSAR, rain thresholds) gives warnings over large areas cheaply and saves lives. Against: Stabilisation (Hong Kong’s slope upgrading, drainage, retaining walls) reduces the hazard itself and protects property; warnings are useless without evacuation plans; planning keeps people away from danger. Conclusion: A combined approach is best: stabilise high-risk slopes in cities, monitor and warn over wider areas, and use planning to reduce exposure.

items.answer: (a) Urban growth on steep slopes; deforestation; road building in mountains; heavier rainfall linked to climate change; more tourism in mountains. (b) Heavy new snow on a weak layer; slopes of 30-45°; warming or rain weakens the pack; wind loading; disturbance by skiers or vibration.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “inclinometer”?
options: A wall built to hold back soil or rock on a slope.
Inserting steel bars into a slope and grouting them to hold the soil together.
An instrument that measures the widening of cracks or the distance between points on a slope.
An instrument in a borehole that measures slope movement at depth.
items.answer: An instrument in a borehole that measures slope movement at depth.
items.markingKey: Inclinometer: an instrument in a borehole that measures slope movement at depth. [1]

items.stem: Explain why planning may be more effective than engineering in LICs.
items.answer: Engineering is expensive; hazard mapping and land-use zoning that keep people off dangerous slopes are cheaper; community warning schemes; but enforcement in informal settlements is difficult.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A student writes: “Engineering can remove landslide risk completely.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “Hong Kong’s slope safety programme reduced landslide deaths.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. It reduces risk but extreme events can still cause failures. (b) Correct. Deaths fell sharply after systematic slope registration and upgrading.

items.stem: Fig. 10.3 shows the cumulative displacement (mm) recorded by an extensometer on a slope above a road in Hong Kong: day 0: 0, day 7: 1.4, day 14: 3.5, day 21: 7, day 28: 11.2, day 35: 19.6. Engineers issue an alert when the rate of movement exceeds 1.5 mm per day. Explain why an increasing rate of movement is a warning sign.
items.answer: Acceleration shows that shear strength is falling relative to stress, often as water pressure rises or a slip surface develops, and may precede rapid failure.

items.stem: Fig. 10.3 shows the cumulative displacement (mm) recorded by an extensometer on a landslide above a village in the Swiss Alps: day 0: 0, day 7: 4.9, day 14: 12.6, day 21: 21.7, day 28: 30.8, day 35: 39.9. items.answer: (a) None: the rate never exceeded the threshold. (b) Install drainage to lower pore pressure; build a retaining wall or use soil nails and anchors; regrade to a lower angle; plant vegetation.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why earthquakes trigger landslides. (b) Explain how deforestation increases landslide risk.
items.answer: (a) Shaking adds a horizontal force (increasing shear stress) and can cause liquefaction or fracturing that reduces shear strength. (b) Roots that bind soil decay; interception and transpiration fall, so more water reaches and stays in the soil, raising pore pressure.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student writes: “Landslides are always caused by a single trigger.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain how deforestation increases landslide risk.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Slopes become progressively weaker; a trigger causes failure of an already unstable slope. (b) Roots that bind soil decay; interception and transpiration fall, so more water reaches and stays in the soil, raising pore pressure.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) [3]

items.stem: Table 10.1 shows four rainstorms on a hillside in Nepal (duration in hours, mean intensity in mm/h): storm A: 3 h, 5.8 mm/h; storm B: 24 h, 1.7 mm/h; storm C: 6 h, 4.4 mm/h; storm D: 2 h, 14.7 mm/h. A global threshold for shallow landslides is I = 14.82 D^−0.39, where I is intensity (mm/h) and D is duration (h). Explain why the threshold intensity falls as storm duration increases.
items.answer: Long storms progressively saturate the soil and raise the water table, so a lower intensity is enough to raise pore-water pressure to the point of failure.

items.stem: “Human activity is now the main cause of mass movement hazards.” Discuss. In your answer you may refer to earthquakes and rainfall.
items.answer: For: Deforestation, road building, quarrying, slope loading and informal settlements on steep slopes increase failures (Rio de Janeiro favelas, Hong Kong before 1977, Freetown 2017). Against: Natural factors (steep slopes, weak rocks, monsoon rain, earthquakes like Wenchuan 2008 or Nepal 2015) cause most landslides; humans mainly increase exposure. Conclusion: Natural factors are the underlying causes, but human activity increasingly triggers failures and, above all, puts people at risk.
